<reason>Both sides built coherent, competitive cases, but B did more of the decisive analytical work. A's central asymmetry frame (corrigible friction vs. irreversible death) and its visceral "weapon left at home can't be drawn" mechanism were rhetorically strong, and A answered pressure questions with concrete safeguards (time-bound triggers, oversight boards) and an honest falsifiability concession. However, B repeatedly pressed the core definitional question the motion demands—what does "expansion" actually add beyond existing reasonable-suspicion law—and in B4.4 landed a clean dilemma: A's triggers either already constitute individualized suspicion (no expansion needed) or remain a geographic/temporal dragnet (the very profiling risk B warned about). A's closing, further weakened by being clipped for length, never squarely resolved this dilemma, instead reasserting the asymmetry frame. B also raised a resource-diversion argument (officer time spent on broader searches vs. targeted investigation) that A answered only by asserting powers are "additive," without addressing finite capacity—an unanswered gap. B's cooperation/trust-erosion mechanism was a plausible, grounded causal counter-story that A's "fear already exists" response blunted but did not neutralize. On balance, B did more to complicate A's strongest asymmetry claim and left a live, unresolved burden on what precisely the expansion authorizes, making B's path to victory clearer at the end of the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's B4.4 dilemma—A's proposed triggers are either redundant with existing individualized suspicion or still amount to a geographic dragnet—was the most decisive unanswered pressure point, since A's closing pivoted to the asymmetry framing instead of resolving it.</best_rebuttal>
